summary:
Probably the earliest letter Paul wrote, around AD 50, which would make it the oldest document in the New Testament, older than any gospel. Paul had founded the church in Thessalonica on his second missionary journey, but opposition drove him out within weeks (Acts 17), leaving very new believers to face hostility without him. Blocked from returning, he sent Timothy to check on them; this letter is his response to Timothy's good report.

The first three chapters are relief and affection. Paul recalls how the Thessalonians received the message, defends his conduct among them (no flattery, no greed, but gentleness "like a nursing mother caring for her children," 2:7), and tells them their endurance has been like new life to him. Chapters 4-5 then take up the question troubling them most. Some of their members had died, and the church feared the dead had missed Christ's return entirely. Paul answers: "since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him" (4:14). Grief remains, but not the grief of "the rest, who are without hope" (4:13).

On when Christ will return, Paul refuses to speculate; a thief in the night gives no warning. He asks instead for alert, ordinary faithfulness, ending in a run of short commands: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything, test everything, hold on to the good. Read the letter as the earliest surviving window into a young church learning to grieve and to hope at the same time.
